metadata.title: Bird flu caused the death of Jackie, a California bald eagle who captured hearts

sources.news_title: Beloved Big Bear bald eagle Jackie died of bird flu
sources.text:
Jackie, the Big Bear bald eagle made famous by a webcam’s livestream, died after suffering from multiple ailments and complications, notably Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI), known as the bird flu, experts said Wednesday in announcing her necropsy findings.
The Ojai Raptor Center, which cared for Jackie until her death on Aug. 10, said on social media:
“The necropsy revealed a complex and unusual disease process involving severe, chronic inflammation and ulceration of the stomach, persistent internal bleeding, anemia and secondary bacterial sepsis. Further diagnostic testing confirmed Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) within the affected tissues, identifying the virus as an underlying cause of the severe stomach ulceration. Multiple complications developed over time and ultimately contributed to her decline and death.”
HPAI is an infectious disease that primarily affects birds and has been circulating in wild bird populations throughout the United States. Waterfowl and shorebirds are natural hosts of avian influenza viruses, while eagles and other raptors may be exposed through contact with infected birds or by consuming infected prey, according to the California Department of Fish and Wildlife.
CDFW said in a statement the necropsy was performed by veterinary pathologists at the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance.
“Jackie’s necropsy confirmed Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) as the primary underlying cause of her decline,” Steve Kubiski, Director of Disease Investigations, San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, was quoted as saying in the CDFW statement. “In an uncommon presentation of the virus, the infection caused a severe ulcer in her stomach that led to persistent internal bleeding, anemia and the development of bacterial sepsis.”
“Together, the findings showed that Jackie was suffering from multiple severe and interconnected disease processes that had been developing over time and ultimately led to her decline and death,” said the CDFW statement.
CDFW also said that consistent with protocols to prevent spread of HPAI, Jackie’s remains were cremated by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s National Eagle Repository.
CDFW also reported:
— Jackie was negative for West Nile Virus infection and heavy metals in her system were within acceptable limits and not associated with her disease progression.
–Brodifacoum, known as a rat poison that has been associated with eagle deaths, was detected in her liver. But it was not identified as the primary cause of illness or death.
After her death, but before the necropsy results came in, the Ojai center reported Jackie had been suffering from health problems including large blood clots in both wings and a kidney.
In July, Jackie was rescued after being found grounded following a fight with other eagles.
Jackie was born in 2012 by two Big Bear Eagles, Ricky and Lucy, named by the U.S. Forest Service. Jackie fledged from the nest later that summer. Her life and the lives of her mates and chicks were later documented on a livestream nest camera installed by Friends of Big Bear Valley.
Jackie and the other eagles in the nest attracted legions of followers, some fascinated by the parenting adventures of the adult eagles and the antics of their eaglets; and many connecting the eagles to the larger ecosystem and the need to protect it.
“Jackie’s story brought unprecedented public attention to bald eagles and the importance of protecting the habitats they depend on. Her life and the public’s connection to her highlights the powerful role that wildlife can play in connecting people to conservation,” CDFW said in its statement.
CDFW added there was no evidence Jackie’s latest mate, Shadow, or their eaglets were sick.
On Oct. 3, some 2,000 fans and watchers of Jackie participated in a Big Bear event honoring her called “Wings Over Big Bear.”
Last month, Jackie was also honored during events in Fawnskin at what is now called Fawnskin Freedom Park.

sources.news_title: Cause of death for Jackie the bald eagle revealed; avian icon has been cremated
sources.text:
LOS ANGELES — Jackie amassed millions of devoted fans thanks to a nonstop livestream of the aerie overlooking Big Bear Lake she shared with mate Shadow. When Big Bear’s celebrity eagle died in August, questions swirled about what had gone wrong.
The California Department of Fish and Wildlife announced Wednesday that Jackie died from highly pathogenic avian influenza, also known as bird flu. Testing revealed that rat poison was in her system, but officials do not believe it to be the primary cause of her illness or death. She had been suffering from multiple diseases, according to the department.
In July, the eagle was found weak and disheveled on the shoreline of Big Bear Lake. She was taken to Ojai for treatment. Tests revealed she had anemia, so she received a blood transfusion from another eagle. Despite scans and biopsies, experts could not figure out why she was ill. She died on Aug. 10 in the care of the Ojai Raptor Center.
Veterinary pathologists at the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance performed the necropsy, Fish and Wildlife said in a joint statement with the wildlife alliance and the raptor center.
The necropsy found that highly pathogenic avian influenza was the “primary underlying cause of her decline,” and that the infection caused a severe stomach ulcer.
Jackie also showed signs of chronic disease involving the ventriculus, also known as the gizzard. The disease contributed to blood loss, anemia and a serious secondary bacterial infection. A toxicology screening discovered brodifacoum — rat poison — in her liver, as well as other persistent environmental contaminants.
“The necropsy did not find uncontrolled bleeding typically associated with anticoagulant rodenticide; therefore, brodifacoum was not identified as the primary cause of illness or death,” Fish and Wildlife said.
Experts have also ruled out West Nile virus and heavy metals as factors that could have contributed to her death.
“The necropsy results have helped connect many of the findings we were seeing throughout the eagle’s hospitalization,” Chris Eksteen, executive director of the Ojai Raptor Center, said in the statement.
Jackie’s remains were cremated by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s National Eagle Repository to prevent the spread of bird flu, according to Fish and Wildlife.
Some Jackie fans had unsuccessfully fought officials’ plans to send Jackie to the repository, which was established in the 1970s to provide members of federally recognized Native American tribes with eagle feathers, parts and whole bodies for religious use. At the time, fans argued that Jackie deserved special treatment (virtually all recovered carcasses of bald and golden eagles in the country are sent to the facility) and that she should perhaps be preserved through taxidermy.
Fish and Wildlife Service and its National Eagle Repository did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Jackie’s longtime mate, Shadow, remains in Big Bear and appears to be healthy, Fish and Wildlife said. Days after Jackie’s death, Shadow was spotted in the company of a different female.

sources.news_title: Big Bear bald eagle Jackie's cause of death revealed in new necropsy report
sources.text:
BIG BEAR, Calif. (KABC) -- Big Bear's beloved bald eagle Jackie died from complications related to a type of infectious avian flu, according to necropsy results.
The California Department of Fish and Wildlife, San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance and Ojai Raptor Center on Wednesday released the results of testing conducted after Jackie's death, shedding new light on the illness that veterinarians had been trying to diagnose during weeks of treatment.
The findings determined that highly pathogenic avian influenza, or bird flu, was the primary underlying cause of Jackie's decline.
"Jackie's necropsy confirmed Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) as the primary underlying cause of her decline," said Steve Kubiski, director of disease investigations for the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance. "In an uncommon presentation of the virus, the infection caused a severe ulcer in her stomach that led to persistent internal bleeding, anemia, and the development of bacterial sepsis."
The damage also allowed bacteria to enter her body, resulting in a serious secondary infection. Additional testing found evidence of the virus in multiple tissues.
The results help explain the severe anemia that veterinarians were battling while caring for Jackie at the Ojai Raptor Center earlier this year. Jackie spent more than three weeks receiving intensive treatment, including oxygen therapy and a life-saving blood transfusion, as experts worked to determine what was making her sick.
Toxicology testing detected brodifacoum, a rodent poison, in Jackie's liver. However, officials said the findings did not show the type of uncontrolled bleeding associated with the poison, and it was not identified as the primary cause of her illness or death.
"The necropsy results have helped connect many of the findings we were seeing throughout the eagle's hospitalization," said Chris Eksteen, executive director of Ojai Raptor Center. "We are grateful to the many veterinary specialists, laboratories, wildlife agencies and partner organizations who worked alongside our team to understand her illness and provide her with the best possible care. Caring for her was an extraordinary privilege for our entire team."
Jackie died Aug. 10 after her condition continued to deteriorate despite treatment. Her remains were later cremated by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's National Eagle Repository, according to wildlife officials.
"The story of the Big Bear bald eagle reflects the powerful connection people feel to these iconic birds," said CDFW Director Meghan Hertel. "We're grateful to everyone who cared for her and worked to support her well-being. Understanding the results of these tests is an important part of learning from this case and can help inform the care and treatment of other eagles and wildlife in the future."
Jackie's death marked the loss of one half of the iconic bald eagle pair that had occupied Big Bear Valley for years. Her mate, Shadow, remains in the area, and officials said there is no evidence that he or the pair's eaglets became sick.
Jackie gained a worldwide following through the Friends of Big Bear Valley eagle camera, with millions of viewers tuning in over the years to watch her and Shadow raise their young. Wildlife officials said her story helped bring attention to bald eagles, conservation and the habitats they depend on.

sources.news_title: Bald eagle Jackie confirmed to have died from bird flu-caused sepsis
Jackie the celebrity bald eagle died of bird flu, California officials confirm
sources.text:
The California Department of Fish and Wildlife confirmed on Wednesday that the primary cause of Jackie’s death was highly pathogenic avian influenza, commonly referred to as bird flu. While a toxicology screen detected rodenticide in her system, state wildlife officials concluded it was not the main reason for her death. Instead, a post-mortem examination revealed she was battling several overlapping medical conditions.
Jackie was first rescued in July after being found weakened and unkempt near the Big Bear Lake shore. She was transported to the Ojai Raptor Center for emergency care, where diagnostics showed severe anemia that required a blood transfusion from a donor eagle. Despite extensive imaging and biopsies, medical experts were initially unable to pinpoint the underlying cause of her illness. She passed away on August 10 while receiving care at the Ojai facility.
Also read: The 'biggest' risk to Asia’s economies isn’t over yet, IMF warns
A necropsy was subsequently performed by veterinary pathologists at the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, coordinated jointly with the Ojai Raptor Center and the state wildlife department.
The examination identified bird flu as the “primary underlying cause of her decline,” determining that the viral infection had triggered a severe stomach ulcer.
Pathologists also noted chronic disease in her ventriculus (gizzard), which had caused internal bleeding, severe anemia, and a critical secondary bacterial infection. While testing revealed the anticoagulant rat poison brodifacoum and other persistent environmental toxins in her liver, officials clarified the rodenticide's impact.
“The necropsy did not find uncontrolled bleeding typically associated with anticoagulant rodenticide; therefore, brodifacoum was not identified as the primary cause of illness or death,” Fish and Wildlife noted in its official release.
Additionally, investigators ruled out heavy metal toxicity and West Nile virus as contributing factors.
Reflecting on the final report, Chris Eksteen, executive director of the Ojai Raptor Center, stated, “The necropsy results have helped connect many of the findings we were seeing throughout the eagle’s hospitalization.”
Also read: World Health Organization informs countries to improve efforts to prevent lead exposure
To manage biosecurity risks and eliminate the threat of spreading avian influenza, Jackie’s remains were cremated by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s National Eagle Repository, state officials confirmed.
This outcome followed an effort by dedicated fans who lobbied against sending Jackie to the repository, a federally mandated facility created in the 1970s to distribute eagle feathers and remains to enrolled Native American tribe members for ceremonial use. Supporters argued that the famed eagle deserved an exception to the standard national protocol for recovered eagle carcasses, suggesting she instead be preserved through taxidermy.
Representatives from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Eagle Repository did not immediately reply to requests for comment.
Meanwhile, Jackie’s long-term nesting partner, Shadow, appears in good health and remains in the Big Bear area. State wildlife officials noted that just days after Jackie’s passing, Shadow was observed alongside a new female eagle.

Cause of death of beloved bald eagle, Jackie, revealed
Officials have revealed the cause of death of Jackie, the beloved California bald eagle whose life was watched by millions around the world via video livestreams.
The California Department of Fish and Wildlife released the results of the necropsy and additional diagnostic testing, revealing the bald eagle from the Big Bear Valley died from avian influenza complications.

"Jackie's necropsy confirmed Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) as the primary underlying cause of her decline," Director of Disease Investigations, San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, Steve Kubiski, said in the report. "In an uncommon presentation of the virus, the infection caused a severe ulcer in her stomach that led to persistent internal bleeding, anemia, and the development of bacterial sepsis."
Jackie was also said to have shown signs of "chronic disease involving the ventriculus, the muscular portion of a bird’s stomach, commonly called the gizzard," the release said. A toxicology screening also detected brodifacoum, an anticoagulant rodenticide, in the liver, as well as persistent environmental contaminants.
Jackie had been nesting in the Big Bear area for years, where she and her partner, Shadow, raised eaglets together. Their nest sat high in a Jeffrey pine tree near Big Bear Lake, more than 7,000 feet above sea level.
Jackie, who died on Aug. 10, 2026, became especially popular for her dedicated parenting, dramatic interactions with Shadow and the challenges she faced protecting eggs and chicks from harsh mountain weather.
Shadow, the release said, remains in Big Bear, California. Wildlife officials said that there is nothing to indicate he or their eaglets, Sandy and Luna, are sick.
"Jackie's story brought unprecedented public attention to bald eagles and the importance of protecting the habitats they depend on," the CDFW said. "Her life and the public's connection to her highlights the powerful role that wildlife can play in connecting people to conservation."

sources.news_title: Jackie the bald eagle’s final cause of death revealed
sources.text:
The Ojai Raptor Center released the final necropsy results for Jackie, an internet-famous bald eagle mother who was in their care this summer. Jackie was brought into the bird rehabilitation center weak and dehydrated following an altercation with another eagle in July.
Officially designated as Patient 26-519, Jackie’s necropsy revealed a “complex and unusual disease process involving severe, chronic inflammation and ulceration of the stomach, persistent internal bleeding, anemia and secondary bacterial sepsis.” She was also diagnosed with Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) commonly called bird flu, which was behind severe stomach ulceration. Raptors (eagles, hawks, falcons, owls, etc.) are highly susceptible to the virus
All of these medical complications developed over time and ultimately contributed to her death on August 10.
“These findings have helped connect many of the pieces we were seeing throughout her hospitalization and provided a better understanding of the challenges she faced,” the Ojai Raptor Center wrote. “We are grateful to the many veterinary specialists, laboratories, wildlife agencies and partner organizations who worked alongside our team to understand her illness and provide her with the best possible care. Caring for her was an extraordinary privilege for our entire team.”
The full report can be read in Jackie’s veterinary medical journal. The necropsy was preformed by veterinary pathologists at the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance.
Friends of Big Bear Valley (FOBBV), the non-profit organization that runs the live cameras where viewers from all over the world watched Jackie and her partner Shadow, said that they will follow up with their thoughts once their team has had time to process the report.
“The story of the Big Bear bald eagle reflects the powerful connection people feel to these iconic birds,” California Department of Fish and Wildlife Director Meghan Hertel added. “We’re grateful to everyone who cared for her and worked to support her well-being. Understanding the results of these tests is an important part of learning from this case and can help inform the care and treatment of other eagles and wildlife in the future.”
Jackie’s story
Jackie was born, raised, and lived in Big Bear Valley in Southern California. Prior to the 2011-2012 nesting season, no bald eagle chicks were known to have ever hatched in Big Bear Valley. Then came Jackie, named after a forest ranger and born to parents Ricky and Lucy in 2012.
During the 2016-2017 nesting season, Jackie took over a nest where Friends of Big Bear Valley (FOBBV) had a camera stationed. In 2018, she had two chicks named Stormy and Big Bear Baby (or BBB) with her first mate, Mr. B.
Her long-time partner Shadow entered the picture in summer 2018. He showed up at the nest and would not leave. FOBBV called the new male Shadow because he appeared so determined to stay in the nest, and the team initially believed he was one of Jackie’s siblings, also named Shadow. The eagle’s plumage indicated he was one year older than the other Shadow and not Jackie’s sibling, but the name stuck.
Shadow continued to hold his ground and Mr. B gave up and eventually left. Jackie then accepted Shadow as her new mate.
Wildlife cameras documented Jackie and Shadow’s life together, offering viewers a direct look into the brutality and beauty of nature. The pair successfully raised chicks in 2019 (Cookie and Simba) and 2022 (Spirit). The pair’s eggs failed to hatch in 2023 and 2024. In 2025, Jackie laid three eggs that all hatched in early March. However, a strong snowstorm dumped up to two feet of snow and battered the nest with strong wind and only two of the chicks (Sunny and Gizmo) survived.
In January, Jackie laid two eggs in the nest, but ravens destroyed them. She later laid two more eggs that hatched in April and named Luna and Sandy. The name Sandy is in honor of FOBBV’s former executive director Sandy Steers who died from cancer in February.
Jackie’s injury and death
On July 17, Jackie was found injured on the ground near Dana Point Park, California. Cell phone video from a witness confirmed that she had an altercation with two other subadult eagles. She successfully fended off the other eagles by turning over and using her talons, but could not fly far away.
She was transferred to the Ojai Raptor Center, where she was diagnosed with severe anemia. Her anemia worsened during the first week of August, the Ojai Raptor Center said that she was in unstable condition on August 9. Her packed cell volume (PCV) fell below percent, before rising to nine percent.

She was transferred to the Ojai Raptor Center for care, where she was diagnosed with severe anemia. Her anemia worsened during the first week of August, the Ojai Raptor Center said that she was in unstable condition on August 9. Her packed cell volume (PCV) fell below percent, before rising to nine percent. 
Jackie died early in the morning on August 10. The necropsy did not reveal a single cause of death, and instead pointed to several factors including severe anemia, blood clots in her wing and one kidney, and liver and lung abnormalities.
Jackie’s resilience inspired millions of people around the world. To honor her memory, FOBBV accepts donations to support its conservation efforts in the area. Supporters can also donate to Ojai Raptor Center’s Bald Eagle Recovery Campaign.

BIG BEAR LAKE, Calif. — Bird flu caused the death of a bald eagle named Jackie who had become an internet sensation and a symbol of the species' recovery in California, officials said.
A necropsy and additional testing found that the primary underlying cause of Jackie's death in August was highly pathogenic avian influenza, the California Department of Fish and Wildlife said Wednesday in a news release.
In the weeks before she died, Jackie was being treated at the Ojai Raptor Center for various ailments, including anemia. Chris Eksteen, the center's director, said in the news release that the necropsy results “have helped connect many of the findings” they saw during her hospitalization.
“In an uncommon presentation of the virus, the infection caused a severe ulcer in her stomach that led to persistent internal bleeding, anemia, and the development of bacterial sepsis," Steve Kubiski, the disease investigations director at the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, where the necropsy was conducted, said in the news release.
For more than a decade, nature lovers watched via an online video feed as Jackie and her partner, Shadow, tended to their nest each year atop trees near Big Bear Lake in the San Bernardino Mountains east of Los Angeles. There's no evidence Shadow is ill, according to the news release.
The nonprofit Friends of Big Bear Valley installed the nest camera in 2015 and documented the successes and failures of each breeding season.
Highly pathogenic avian influenza has been circulating in bird populations throughout the U.S. While waterfowl and shorebirds are natural hosts for bird flu viruses, eagles and other raptors can be exposed through contact with infected birds or by eating them, according to the news release.
Jackie's remains were cremated to prevent transmission of the virus, it said.
American bald eagles teetered on the brink of extinction until the pesticide DDT was banned in the 1970s and other protections were established, leading the species to rebound and be removed from the federal endangered list.

Bird Flu Confirmed as Primary Cause of Death for Big Bear Bald Eagle Jackie, Final Necropsy Reveals - Victor Valley News
sources.text:
Bird Flu Confirmed as Primary Cause of Death for Big Bear Bald Eagle Jackie, Final Necropsy Reveals
BIG BEAR, Calif. (VVNG.com) — Highly pathogenic bird flu was the primary underlying cause of death for Jackie, the beloved bald eagle from Big Bear Valley, according to final necropsy findings released by the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) and additional information shared by the Ojai Raptor Center.
The findings revealed that the virus caused an unusual and severe medical condition involving stomach ulceration, persistent internal bleeding, anemia and a secondary bacterial infection that ultimately contributed to Jackie’s decline and death.
In a written statement, CDFW announced the results in partnership with the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance and Ojai Raptor Center, following extensive laboratory testing and toxicology screenings.
The necropsy was performed by veterinary pathologists at the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance and provided new insight into the complicated illness that affected Jackie during her hospitalization.
“Jackie’s necropsy confirmed Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) as the primary underlying cause of her decline,” said Steve Kubiski, director of disease investigations at the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance. “In an uncommon presentation of the virus, the infection caused a severe ulcer in her stomach that led to persistent internal bleeding, anemia, and the development of bacterial sepsis.”
According to CDFW, Jackie showed signs of chronic disease affecting the ventriculus, the muscular portion of a bird’s stomach commonly known as the gizzard.
The damaged and ulcerated tissue contributed to ongoing blood loss and persistent severe anemia. The damaged tissue also allowed bacteria to enter her body, resulting in a serious secondary bacterial infection known as sepsis.
Veterinary specialists also discovered severe inflammation and blood clot formation in Jackie’s heart and several major blood vessels.
Additional diagnostic testing confirmed the presence of bird flu viral genetic material in multiple tissues throughout her body, including the ulcerated portion of her stomach.
In its own statement titled “Final Necropsy Findings for Bald Eagle Patient 26-519,” the Ojai Raptor Center provided additional context about the findings and the medical challenges Jackie faced.
The center explained that the necropsy revealed a complex and unusual disease process involving severe, chronic stomach inflammation and ulceration, persistent internal bleeding, anemia and secondary bacterial sepsis.
Further testing confirmed highly pathogenic bird flu within the affected tissues, identifying the virus as an underlying cause of the severe stomach ulceration.
According to the center, multiple medical complications developed over time and ultimately contributed to Jackie’s decline and death.
The findings also helped the veterinary team better understand the symptoms and complications observed throughout her hospitalization.
“These findings have helped connect many of the pieces we were seeing throughout her hospitalization and provided a better understanding of the challenges she faced,” the Ojai Raptor Center stated.
The organization also expressed appreciation for the specialists and agencies involved in Jackie’s treatment.
“We are grateful to the many veterinary specialists, laboratories, wildlife agencies and partner organizations who worked alongside our team to understand her illness and provide her with the best possible care. Caring for her was an extraordinary privilege for our entire team,” the center said in its statement.
Additional Testing Detected Rodenticide but Did Not Identify It as Primary Cause
As part of the investigation, veterinary specialists conducted additional testing to determine whether other illnesses or environmental toxins contributed to Jackie’s condition.
Testing showed Jackie was negative for West Nile virus, while heavy metal levels, including lead, were within acceptable limits and were not associated with the identified disease progression.
Toxicology screening detected brodifacoum, an anticoagulant rodenticide used in some rat poisons, in Jackie’s liver. Persistent environmental contaminants were also identified.
However, the necropsy did not reveal the uncontrolled bleeding typically associated with anticoagulant rodenticide exposure.
As a result, investigators did not identify brodifacoum as the primary cause of Jackie’s illness or death.
Instead, the combined findings indicated that Jackie had been suffering from multiple severe and interconnected medical conditions that developed over time, with highly pathogenic bird flu identified as the primary underlying cause.
Ojai Raptor Center Updates Information About Jackie’s Medical Care
The Ojai Raptor Center said it has updated the frequently asked questions section of its website dedicated to Patient 26-519, the identification number assigned to Jackie during her medical care.
The updated information provides additional details about the necropsy findings and the treatment she received during her hospitalization.
The organization encouraged those following Jackie’s story to visit the Patient 26-519 section of its website for more information.
The center said it will continue sharing important updates with the community as they become available.
Jackie’s Remains Cremated Following Bird Flu Findings
According to CDFW, Jackie’s remains were cremated by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s National Eagle Repository.
The cremation was conducted in accordance with established procedures intended to prevent the transmission of highly pathogenic bird flu to wildlife or humans.
“The story of the Big Bear bald eagle reflects the powerful connection people feel to these iconic birds,” said CDFW Director Meghan Hertel. “We’re grateful to everyone who cared for her and worked to support her well-being. Understanding the results of these tests is an important part of learning from this case and can help inform the care and treatment of other eagles and wildlife in the future.”
Highly pathogenic bird flu is an infectious disease that primarily affects birds and has been circulating among wild bird populations throughout the United States.
Waterfowl and shorebirds are natural hosts of bird flu viruses, while bald eagles and other birds of prey may become exposed through contact with infected birds or by consuming infected prey.
Shadow Remains in Big Bear Valley
Jackie’s death marked the loss of one half of the iconic bald eagle pair that had occupied Big Bear Valley for years.
Her longtime mate, Shadow, remains in Big Bear Valley.
According to CDFW, available camera data has shown no evidence that Shadow or the eaglets were sick.
Jackie’s life and the public’s connection to her brought significant attention to bald eagles and the importance of protecting the habitats they depend on.
Wildlife officials said the findings from her necropsy could help inform future care and treatment of other eagles and wildlife facing similar illnesses.
Additional information about Jackie’s medical history and final necropsy findings is available through the Ojai Raptor Center’s Patient 26-519 webpage, which the organization directs visitors to through the Linktree in its social media profile.
CDFW also previously released an update on Jackie’s condition and medical care.

CDFW added there was no evidence Jackie’s latest mate, Shadow, or their eaglets were sick.
With details surrounding Jackie’s death now revealed, fans may have a chance to reach some semblance of closure.
“I imagine she might’ve been sick for a while, but for her to push through and make sure her eaglets fledged. She was a wonderful mother,” Christy Spraggins LaBrec wrote on a Friends of Big Bear Valley Facebook post announcing that the necropsy report had been released.
“As wonderful and beautiful as nature and wildlife is, it’s also extremely hard,” Kat Woody also wrote. “Jackie proved what life, love and survival mean. We should all learn from her example. She was a force of nature and a treasure in every way.”
On Oct. 3, some 2,000 fans and watchers of Jackie participated in a Big Bear event honoring her called “Wings Over Big Bear.”
Last month, Jackie was also honored during events in Fawnskin at what is now called Fawnskin Freedom Park.
“We just don’t know what this season is going to hold for us,” Voisard said.
Shadow has recently been spending time with a younger adult eagle, banded “KD1” by the Orange County Water District and known as “Kaydee” by Friends.
“Life goes on and forward, and that’s part of Jackie’s legacy: resilience, strength, taking care of your family and the people around you,” Voisard said.

sources.news_title: Big Bear bald eagle Jackie's cause of death revealed
sources.text:
Big Bear bald eagle Jackie's cause of death revealed
Big Bear bald eagle Jackie's cause of death has been revealed nearly two months after she died in August, following weeks of testing and rehabilitation.
According to the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, a necropsy and additional testing determined that Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza, or HPAI, was the "primary underlying cause of her decline."
"In an uncommon presentation of the virus, the infection caused a severe ulcer in her stomach that led to persistent internal bleeding, anemia, and the development of bacterial sepsis," said Steve Kubiski, the Director of Disease Investigations with the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, which performed the necropsy.
Jackie, who was estimated to be around 14 years old, died nearly a month after she was rescued from the Big Bear Lake shoreline, where she was found after being seen in a fight with two subadult eagles in July.
A team of veterinary experts at the Ojai Raptor Center oversaw her care in the weeks that followed, documenting the process as they tried to nurse her back to health. Despite undergoing a blood transfusion, which briefly provided a glimpse of hope, Jackie continued to suffer setbacks in her recovery due to the sickness, which remained a mystery until Wednesday's announcement by California wildlife officials.
"Jackie showed signs of chronic disease involving the ventriculus, the muscular portion of a bird's stomach, commonly called the gizzard. The damaged and ulcerated tissue contributed to ongoing blood loss and her persistent severe anemia," the CDFW release said. "It also allowed bacteria to enter the body, resulting in a serious secondary bacterial infection."
Officials said that additional testing also revealed severe inflammation and blood clot formation in Jackie's heart and several major blood vessels, and that the HPAI virus genetic material was present in several tissues throughout her body, including the ulcerated tissue in her ventriculus. Other tests showed Jackie was negative for West Nile Virus, and heavy metal levels were within acceptable limits.
While toxicology screening detected brodifacoum, an anticoagulant rodenticide, in Jackie's liver, the necropsy did not find uncontrolled bleeding typically associated with the chemical pesticide, so it was not identified as her primary cause of illness or death.
"Together, the findings showed that Jackie was suffering from multiple severe and interconnected disease processes that had been developing over time and ultimately led to her decline and death," CDFW's release said.
Jackie's remains were cremated by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's National Eagle Repository, following the established procedures intended to prevent the transmission of HPAI to wildlife or humans, the release said.
"The story of the Big Bear bald eagle reflects the powerful connection people feel to these iconic birds," said a statement from CDFW Director Meghan Hertel. "We're grateful to everyone who cared for her and worked to support her well-being. Understanding the results of these tests is an important part of learning from this case and can help inform the care and treatment of other eagles and wildlife in the future."
Jackie was an iconic fixture in Southern California, drawing the attention of millions across the United States thanks to the 24/7 livestream camera documenting her life and that of her partner, Shadow, from above Big Bear Lake. Over the years, the duo parented several clutches of eaglets, most recently Sandy and Luna.
CDFW officials said that based on camera data, they have no evidence to suggest that Shadow or the eaglets were sick.
"Jackie's story brought unprecedented public attention to bald eagles and the importance of protecting the habitats they depend on," the release from CDFW said. "Her life and the public's connection to her highlights the powerful role that wildlife can play in connecting people to conservation."
In the weeks since her death, Jackie has been honored with a massive memorial service in Big Bear, a life-size monument at a park in the San Bernardino Mountains and an Ontario Tower Buzzers minor league baseball game dedicated to celebrating her life. California state legislators also passed a resolution in her honor, proclaiming September 4 as California Wildlife Day.

Avian Influenza identified as primary underlying cause of Big Bear bald eagle Jackie’s decline
BIG BEAR, Calif. (KESQ) - The final necropsy report on Jackie the Big Bear bald eagle's death was released on Wednesday, revealing Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza as the underlying primary cause of her decline.
"The necropsy, performed by veterinary pathologists at the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, along with extensive additional laboratory and toxicology testing, provided new information about the complex medical condition that led to Jackie’s decline and death," reads a news release by the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW).
Jackie died on August 10 after more than three weeks of intensive medical care at the Ojai Raptor Center.
Officials said the "necropsy revealed a complex and unusual disease process involving severe, chronic inflammation and ulceration of the stomach, persistent internal bleeding, anemia and secondary bacterial sepsis."
Further diagnostic testing confirmed Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) within the affected tissues.
HPAI is an infectious disease that primarily affects birds and has been circulating in wild bird populations throughout the United States, the CDFW reports. Waterfowl and shorebirds are natural hosts of avian influenza viruses, while eagles and other raptors may be exposed through contact with infected birds or by consuming infected prey.
Officials identified HPAI as an underlying cause of Jackie's severe stomach ulceration. Multiple complications developed over time and ultimately contributed to her decline and death.
"Jackie's necropsy confirmed Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) as the primary underlying cause of her decline," said Steve Kubiski, Director of Disease Investigations, San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance. "In an uncommon presentation of the virus, the infection caused a severe ulcer in her stomach that led to persistent internal bleeding, anemia, and the development of bacterial sepsis."
The agency added that Jackie showed signs of chronic disease involving the ventriculus, the muscular portion of a bird’s stomach, commonly called the gizzard. The damaged and ulcerated tissue contributed to ongoing blood loss and her persistent severe anemia.
It also allowed bacteria to enter the body, resulting in a serious secondary bacterial infection.
Severe inflammation and blood clot formation were also found in the heart and several major blood vessels. Follow-up testing showed that HPAI virus genetic material was present in several tissues throughout her body, including the ulcerated tissue in the ventriculus.
Together, the findings showed that Jackie was suffering from multiple severe and interconnected disease processes that had been developing over time and ultimately led to her decline and death.
“The necropsy results have helped connect many of the findings we were seeing throughout the eagle’s hospitalization,” said Chris Eksteen, Executive Director of Ojai Raptor Center. “We are grateful to the many veterinary specialists, laboratories, wildlife agencies and partner organizations who worked alongside our team to understand her illness and provide her with the best possible care. Caring for her was an extraordinary privilege for our entire team.”
Consistent with established procedures intended to prevent the transmission of HPAI to wildlife or humans, Jackie's remains were cremated by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s National Eagle Repository.
